Build a layout row by row

Source: R/nodes.R
new_row.Rd

new_row() adds a row of plots below everything built so far, new_column() adds a column of plots to the right of it, and new_grid() adds a grid of plots below it. Together they build a figure step by step:

Usage

new_row(..., wrap = NULL, horizontal_align = "left", vertical_align = "bottom")

new_column(..., wrap = NULL, horizontal_align = "left", vertical_align = NULL)

new_grid(
  ...,
  ncol = NULL,
  nrow = NULL,
  wrap = NULL,
  horizontal_align = "left",
  vertical_align = "bottom"
)

Arguments

...

A layout (optional, first) followed by ggplots (including tidyplots), grobs, layouts, or other objects that render themselves to a gtable (see as_layout_gtable()), such as tidymontage montages. Lists are spliced, so the output of auto_height() can be passed directly.

wrap

Maximum width in mm (maximum height for new_column()), axis labels, legends and gaps included. NULL (default) never wraps.

  • In new_row(), a row that doesn't fit is broken into several lines, like text in a word processor: each line takes as many plots as fit and is laid out on its own. horizontal_align applies to every line; with "justify" all lines but the last are spread to the width of the widest line. Best for plots of different widths.

  • In new_grid(), the number of columns is chosen as large as possible while the grid fits. All rows share the same columns, so this is best for plots of similar widths (small multiples). Can't be combined with ncol or nrow.

  • In new_column(), a column that is too tall is broken into several columns side by side, like newspaper columns. vertical_align (default "top" here) applies within every column; with "justify" all columns but the last are spread to the height of the tallest one. Tags run down each column before moving to the next.

A plot larger than wrap gets a line (column) of its own.

horizontal_align

Where leftover horizontal space in the new row (column, grid) goes: "left" (default), "right", "center" or "justify" (between its plots).

vertical_align

Where leftover vertical space goes: "bottom" (default), "top", "center" or "justify" (between its plots). For new_column() with wrap, the default is "top".

ncol, nrow

Number of grid columns and rows. Cells are filled row-wise.

Value

A layout.

Details

new_row(p1, p2) |>
  new_row(p3, p4) |>
  new_column(p5) |>
  new_column(p6) |>
  new_row(p7)

Starting and adding. If the first argument is a layout, the new row (column, grid) is added to it. Otherwise, a new layout is started, so new_row(p1, p2) is simply a row of p1 and p2. To start a new row with an existing layout as its first element, wrap it in a list: new_row(list(inner), p3). Several plots in one call form one row (column): new_column(p5, p6) is a single column with p6 below p5, whereas new_column(p5) |> new_column(p6) gives two columns side by side. Layouts can also be passed as elements, e.g. new_column(new_grid(...)) puts a grid to the right.

Panel alignment. Plots are aligned by their panel edges, not by their outer boxes. Within a row, panel bottoms line up by default (so do the x axes); within a column, panel left edges line up (so do the y axes).

Rows vs. grids. Each row is laid out on its own: in new_row(p1, p2) |> new_row(p3, p4), the rows line up at the left edge of their outermost panels, but p2 and p4 need not line up. In new_grid(p1, p2, p3, p4, ncol = 2), every grid column is as wide as its widest panel, so p2 sits exactly above p4. In a grid, NULL leaves an empty cell.

Spare space. When plots have a fixed size, a row (column, grid) often has more space than its plots need. horizontal_align and vertical_align decide where that space goes inside this row: they place its plots and spread space between them. Nested rows, columns and grids always fill the space they are given and arrange their own contents with their own alignment. For example, in new_row(p1, p2) |> new_row(p3, p4, horizontal_align = "justify") the lower row spans the full width of the upper row, with the extra space between p3 and p4.

Examples

p1 <- dummy(name = "p1", color = "#0072B2")
p2 <- dummy(name = "p2", color = "#D55E00")
p3 <- dummy(name = "p3", color = "#009E73")
p4 <- dummy(name = "p4", color = "#E69F00")
p5 <- dummy(name = "p5", color = "#56B4E9", height = NA)
p6 <- dummy(name = "p6", color = "#F5C710", height = NA)
p7 <- dummy(name = "p7", color = "#DD227D", width = NA)
wide <- dummy(name = "wide", color = "#009E73", width = 45)

new_row(p1, p2) |>
  new_row(p3, p4) |>
  new_column(p5) |>
  new_column(p6) |>
  new_row(p7)


new_grid(p1, p2, p3, p4, ncol = 2) |>
  new_column(p5) |>
  new_row(p7)


# break a long row into lines of at most 100 mm
new_row(p1, p2, p3, p4, p1, p2, wrap = 100)


# as many grid columns as fit into 100 mm
new_grid(p1, p2, p3, p4, p1, p2, wrap = 100)


# columns of at most 80 mm height
new_column(p1, p2, p3, p4, p1, wrap = 80)


# alignment inside a row or column
new_column(wide, p1, horizontal_align = "center")

new_row(wide, wide) |>
  new_row(p1, p2, horizontal_align = "justify")
